params.question: In the depth-based classification of pyoderma, which set of primary lesions indicates involvement at the level of the superficial epidermis?

answers.text: Pustules centred on hair follicles and tender subcutaneous nodules

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pustules centred on hair follicles indicate follicular pyoderma (such as folliculitis or furuncle), where the infection originates in the pilosebaceous unit rather than in the superficial epidermis.

Correct. Superficial epidermal infections such as non-bullous and bullous impetigo produce crusts and flaccid bullae respectively, because the infection is confined to the uppermost layers of the epidermis.
Spreading erythema with induration indicates involvement of the deeper dermis and subcutis, as seen in cellulitis and erysipelas, where the infection extends well beyond the superficial layers.
A fluctuant swelling with a necrotic centre suggests a deep abscess such as a furuncle or carbuncle, involving the subcutaneous tissue around the hair follicle rather than the superficial epidermis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The morphological vocabulary of pyoderma maps directly onto depth: crusts and flaccid bullae = superficial epidermis, pustules and nodules = follicular, and diffuse erythema with induration = deep dermis and subcutis.

Well done. Recognising that crusts and flaccid bullae point to superficial epidermal involvement is the first step in classifying pyoderma by depth — the key to choosing between topical and systemic therapy.

params.question: Which of the following is an appropriate indication for prescribing topical mupirocin or fusidic acid in pyoderma?

answers.text: Widespread bullous impetigo with lesions covering both arms and the trunk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Widespread pyoderma exceeds the scope of topical therapy. When lesions are extensive, systemic antibiotics are needed to achieve adequate tissue drug levels throughout the affected area.

answers.text: A large carbuncle on the back of the neck in a febrile diabetic patient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A carbuncle is a deep, multi-headed follicular infection often accompanied by systemic signs. It requires systemic anti-staphylococcal antibiotics and may need surgical drainage — topical agents cannot penetrate to the depth of infection.

answers.text: Eradication of nasal Staphylococcus aureus carriage in a patient with recurrent furunculosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Nasal S. aureus carriage is a recognised source of recurrent pyoderma. Intranasal mupirocin is used to eradicate carriage, breaking the cycle of re-infection — one of the three specific indications for topical antimicrobials.

answers.text: Cellulitis of the lower limb with ascending lymphangitis and fever

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cellulitis with lymphangitis and systemic features is a deep, spreading infection requiring systemic antibiotics — often parenteral — because the infection extends far beyond the reach of any topical agent.

overallFeedback.feedback: Topical mupirocin and fusidic acid are reserved for three specific situations: a few localised superficial impetigo lesions, early localised folliculitis, and nasal S. aureus carriage eradication. Deep, widespread, or systemically toxic infections always require systemic therapy.

Exactly. Topical antimicrobials have a narrow but important role: localised superficial impetigo, early folliculitis, and nasal carriage eradication. Using them beyond these indications promotes resistance without therapeutic benefit.

interactions.label: A 48-year-old diabetic man presents with an erythematous, mildly swollen forearm

params.question: A 48-year-old diabetic man presents with an erythematous, mildly swollen forearm. The overlying skin changes appear modest, yet he is writhing in pain vastly disproportionate to the visible findings. He is tachycardic and febrile. What should be your immediate clinical priority?

answers.text: Arrange urgent surgical referral for suspected necrotising soft-tissue infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pain out of proportion to surface appearance, systemic toxicity, and rapid progression in a diabetic patient are cardinal warning signs of necrotising soft-tissue infection. Early surgical exploration is the single most important step — delay is the primary cause of mortality.

answers.text: Prescribe oral cloxacillin for presumed cellulitis and schedule a review in 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pain disproportionate to surface findings in a febrile, toxically unwell patient raises the possibility of necrotising soft-tissue infection — treating as simple cellulitis and waiting 48 hours risks a fatal delay in surgical intervention.

answers.text: Obtain a wound swab for culture and sensitivity before initiating any therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While culture may be useful eventually, awaiting results before acting delays life-saving management. In a patient with features suggestive of necrotising infection, time to surgical exploration is the critical determinant of outcome.

answers.text: Apply warm compresses and topical fusidic acid to encourage spontaneous drainage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Warm compresses and topical therapy are appropriate for a superficial, localised pyoderma. In a patient with systemic toxicity and pain out of proportion to surface findings, they are dangerously inadequate and delay definitive surgical management.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a patient's pain far exceeds what the surface appearance would explain, especially with systemic toxicity and risk factors such as diabetes, necrotising soft-tissue infection must be suspected. Urgent surgical referral — not antibiotics alone or watchful waiting — is the critical step.

Well done. Recognising pain out of proportion to visible skin changes as a warning sign of necrotising soft-tissue infection — and referring urgently to surgery — is the life-saving skill this module teaches.
